| [](https://substack.com/redirect/0053f6fa-9fbe-4da9-b7d4-116df738623a?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)|
---|---|---
In 1972, a journalist asked Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai about the impact of the French Revolution. His answer, the story goes, was, "It's too early to say." The line has become a staple of geopolitical commentary. It's a great reminder that revolutions unfold on very long timelines (and that the Chinese generally think about dynamics over the long-term compared vs. the short attention spans of the West). Interestingly, some thought Enlai was being asked about the then-more-recent 1968 student protests that had rocked the country, but whether he was referring to 1789 or 1968, the quote is worth keeping in mind, because, as this weekend's activity showed, the next revolution seems to be underway.
It started with a high school in Creteil. On September 21, the day after their teachers went on strike, students at the Lycee Antoine-de-Saint-Exupery in the Paris suburbs walked out over unfilled teaching posts, classroom sizes of 35, and rooms without enough tables. By the end of the month, more than a thousand lycees were disrupted. On one day in particular, French police had arrested nearly 2,000 people (mostly minors). Within a month, the unrest had grown from just students to include teachers, parents, unions, farmers and Yellow Vest veterans. Hundreds of thousands of people were in the streets and the historic town hall in Limoges, a building that survived two world wars, was burning.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/3f0ea16c-3890-4184-a0f0-f3355e98c670?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
But there's another fire that will prove harder to contain, and simply can't be put out with water or by using tear gas to stop the rioters. I'm referring to the raging bond market fire. France's 10-year government bond yield pushed through 5% this week, a level it hasn't touched since 2002. Yes, France pays more than Germany and the spread has widened. But the part that should worry you is this: France now pays more to borrow than Italy. _Read that again._ The second-largest economy in the eurozone (indeed, a country whose fiscal credibility was a foundation that helped underwrite the euro itself) is thought to be a worse credit risk than the country it spent two decades lecturing.
Public debt stands at roughly 119% of GDP, the highest ratio since 1946, and the finance ministry's own projection has it reaching nearly 122% next year. The deficit is running at 5.4% of GDP against a 3% EU ceiling. The interest bill alone will run about €79 billion this year and €91 billion in 2027, roughly €250 million a day, and more than France spends on defense.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/68e2d839-550d-49d3-992e-ce0a32399060?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
So what's being done to address the situation? The government's budget proposal (a €54 billion "effort" to bring the deficit down to a still-bloated 5%) faces a National Assembly without a governing majority, whose finance committee has already voted it down 31 to 3, in a political environment where half a million people just marched against austerity.
This is the beginnings of a doom loop. The debt is too large to ignore and too expensive to service, but the cuts required to stabilize it are politically impossible to implement. Every failed attempt to cut spending rattles the bond market, which raises borrowing costs, which makes the debt harder to service, which demands more cuts.
The clearly vicious cycle has no end in sight. Why's that? Because the two sides are reading from different ledgers. The students see a state that cannot replace an absent teacher for seven months during an exam year. The bond market sees a state that cannot afford the teachers it already has. Both are right. And a government with no majority, six months from a presidential election, has nothing to offer either one except promises that neither side see as credible. Ministers were told on October 6 to come back with proposals by the end of the month, and 3,000 substitute teachers have been dispatched to the worst-hit schools. The movement knows it's just a gesture (not a budget).
[](https://substack.com/redirect/9ef212d0-0c5d-4d60-be62-a40b2f75793c?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
The demands are not revolutionary, which I believe makes them dangerous. The lycee union's national call named four grievances: (1) not enough teachers and staff, (2) dilapidated buildings, (3) bloated class sizes, and (4) the stress of Parcoursup, the opaque algorithm that sorts 17-year-olds into universities.
Behind those four sit the stories: a pupil who went seven months without a French teacher in a year with a French exam. Temporary classrooms that hit 40°C in last summer's heatwave and -5°C in winter. Portable toilets with no running water. Rats. A school in Saint-Denis where, the students highlight cockroaches. The students aren't wrong. The infrastructure of French public life is visibly deteriorating, and 62% of the French public, according to a Figaro poll, think the movement is justified.
On October 17, the demands widened and the movement expanded. The call for that day was "Yellows and Youth, Our Struggles Meet," and the students joined an ongoing French grievance: affordability. The cost of living, fuel prices pushed up by the Iran war, pensions, wages, and the sense that the state taxes like a Scandinavian nation and provides services like a Mediterranean one. Fifteen hundred shops were destroyed and 3,000 were looted. The government is blaming the far left, the far left is blaming the police, and the only thing everybody in the street agrees on is that the solution to these problems is more money.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/794be32b-4881-4764-b252-4abecb5f5129?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
And that's why I struggle to see an easy solution. There's simple arithmetic that doesn't care about the placards. Every euro for a teacher is a euro the bond market expects to see cut somewhere else. The protesters are asking the state to do what the bond market has said not to do.
The comparison everyone reaches for is the 1968 French "revolution," when students took to the streets, a government was on its heels, and the president suddenly looked old. I think the analogy is wrong, or at least incomplete. Why? Because de Gaulle dissolved the Assembly and called snap elections that he won, France's public debt was a fraction of its GDP, and the country had room to spend its way to calm. Let's not forget that they raised the minimum wage by more than 30%.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/5fd299a3-af0b-42a3-90cb-0a8646ba13c2?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
Macron has none of the options that de Gaulle had. Could he dissolve the Assembly again? Sure, but the last time he tried that, he produced the hung parliament that has contributed to today's problems. He can't spend to solve the problem, because the bond market is watching. He can't credibly promise reform, because his government is the fourth since the last election. And the political calendar means every group (Le Pen's National Rally, Melenchon's France Unbowed, and the Socialists) is laser-focused on positioning, not governing.
Several of my friends who think deeply about geopolitics and geoeconomics have suggested that if the upcoming budget fails, France might have to seek assistance from the International Monetary Fund. The IMF. _For France_. The ECB, meanwhile, has suggested the solution to French problems lies in France. (Christine Lagarde recently noted that "the primary and first solution lies at home in France.") Some of my friends in Europe are more relaxed about this drama, noting that France is "too big to fail." Others suggest it's too big to save.
The next six weeks decide a lot. The Assembly votes on the revenue half of the budget in early November and on the whole package around November 17. There's a fascinating constitutional provision that allows a bill to pass without a vote. Will Lecornu, despite assurances he would never use this provision (Article 49.3), opt for this path? If he does, which seems likely, what happens?
[](https://substack.com/redirect/1a43eb88-cbda-40e1-8f18-4c4952e03d98?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
I believe there are three main possibilities:
**First** , France could muddle through until the upcoming April elections, the government could make some token gestures such as a school reform package, and the real decisions can be deferred until the next administration takes office. Indeed, this is the default path that France seems to revert to but leads to ever higher debt, higher interest to service that debt, and a population that believes the way to get things done is via protest. I believe this is the most likely scenario.
**Second** , the government falls apart because of the budget. This scenario probably means an emergency law keeps spending the same, leading to a sovereign debt crisis, a bailout, and dragging Italy and Spain along for the ride. At that point, France would have to either choose submission to an EU or IMF dictated program or pursue a Brexit style defiance of Brussels.
The **third** scenario is that the budget leads to real reform. Think of this as a real plan to invest in schools, funded by real cuts. The bond market would love this, spreads would plunge, and France's vicious cycle could turn virtuous. Unfortunately, I think this is the least likely scenario.
[](https://substack.com/redirect/516740ad-beae-4aa2-91be-4747dadde47e?j=eyJ1IjoiMWh2cjYwIn0.VBabVq-VHATXCJqsddI7uMpdiTm0WkVanRDZfvCWMkg)
The question for the rest of Europe and for global markets is whether it stays contained. I don't think it does, for three reasons:
1. **France is critical to the euro 's architecture.** The eurozone has always been understood as a core and a periphery, with Germany and France as the core and the crisis-era rescues flowing outward. When France has to raise money more richly than does Italy, the core-periphery map stops making sense. The ECB would have to address problems that it was not designed to address: a potential failure at the core. Its crisis tool are designed to help small countries hit by unwarranted panic, not for a large country whose panic is warranted.
2. **The bond vigilantes reassert control**. France emerges as the first large democracy where the market forced the question of what happens when you can neither raise taxes nor cut spending (nor inflate). The honest answer, the one on display in Paris, is: you pay more, until you can't. The lesson will spread wide and far, and quickly. Expect bond market contagion.
3. **Political ramifications will also spread quickly**. Within days of Creteil, students in Belgium blockaded schools; Italian students declared a "No Meloni Day" and rioting spread across Milan; Greek students pitched tents outside parliament in Athens; students in Tirana attacked the education ministry. Milei's university cuts led millions in Argentina into the streets, and in Germany, there are calls for protests in 21 cities on October 31. The narrative war over what the French unrest _is about_ (fiscal failure, far-left agitation, inbound migration, police brutality) is already a transatlantic one, and whoever wins it will shape elections from Madrid to Berlin.

Zhou Enlai was right. It is too early to say how this ends. But a bond market at 5% portends trouble.

The next French Revolution is underway and the global implications are scary. | | | Oct 25 | | | | | | | | | | | | | | ---|---|--- In 1972, a journalist asked Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai about the impact of the French Revolution. His answer, the story goes, was, "It's too early to say." The line has become a staple of geopolitical commentary. It's a great reminder that revolutions unfold on very long timelines (and that the Chinese generally think about dynamics over the long-term compared vs. the short attention spans of the West). Interestingly, some thought Enlai was being asked about the then-more-recent 1968 student protests that had rocked the country, but whether he was referring to 1789 or 1968, the quote is worth keeping in mind, because, as this weekend's activity showed, the next revolution seems to be underway. It started with a high school in Creteil. On September 21, the day after their teachers went on strike, students at the Lycee Antoine-de-Saint-Exupery in the Paris suburbs walked out over unfilled teaching posts, classroom sizes of 35, and rooms without enough tables. By the end of the month, more than a thousand lycees were disrupted. On one day in particular, French police had arrested nearly 2,000 people (mostly minors). Within a month, the unrest had grown from just students to include teachers, parents, unions, farmers and Yellow Vest veterans. Hundreds of thousands of people were in the streets and the historic town hall in Limoges, a building that survived two world wars, was burning. But there's another fire that will prove harder to contain, and simply can't be put out with water or by using tear gas to stop the rioters. I'm referring to the raging bond market fire. France's 10-year government bond yield pushed through 5% this week, a level it hasn't touched since 2002. Yes, France pays more than Germany and the spread has widened. But the part that should worry you is this: France now pays more to borrow than Italy. Read that again. The second-largest economy in the eurozone (indeed, a country whose fiscal credibility was a foundation that helped underwrite the euro itself) is thought to be a worse credit risk than the country it spent two decades lecturing. Public debt stands at roughly 119% of GDP, the highest ratio since 1946, and the finance ministry's own projection has it reaching nearly 122% next year. The deficit is running at 5.4% of GDP against a 3% EU ceiling. The interest bill alone will run about €79 billion this year and €91 billion in 2027, roughly €250 million a day, and more than France spends on defense. So what's being done to address the situation? The government's budget proposal (a €54 billion "effort" to bring the deficit down to a still-bloated 5%) faces a National Assembly without a governing majority, whose finance committee has already voted it down 31 to 3, in a political environment where half a million people just marched against austerity. This is the beginnings of a doom loop. The debt is too large to ignore and too expensive to service, but the cuts required to stabilize it are politically impossible to implement. Every failed attempt to cut spending rattles the bond market, which raises borrowing costs, which makes the debt harder to service, which demands more cuts. The clearly vicious cycle has no end in sight. Why's that? Because the two sides are reading from different ledgers. The students see a state that cannot replace an absent teacher for seven months during an exam year. The bond market sees a state that cannot afford the teachers it already has. Both are right. And a government with no majority, six months from a presidential election, has nothing to offer either one except promises that neither side see as credible. Ministers were told on October 6 to come back with proposals by the end of the month, and 3,000 substitute teachers have been dispatched to the worst-hit schools. The movement knows it's just a gesture (not a budget). The demands are not revolutionary, which I believe makes them dangerous. The lycee union's national call named four grievances: (1) not enough teachers and staff, (2) dilapidated buildings, (3) bloated class sizes, and (4) the stress of Parcoursup, the opaque algorithm that sorts 17-year-olds into universities. Behind those four sit the stories: a pupil who went seven months without a French teacher in a year with a French exam. Temporary classrooms that hit 40°C in last summer's heatwave and -5°C in winter. Portable toilets with no running water. Rats. A school in Saint-Denis where, the students highlight cockroaches. The students aren't wrong. The infrastructure of French public life is visibly deteriorating, and 62% of the French public, according to a Figaro poll, think the movement is justified. On October 17, the demands widened and the movement expanded. The call for that day was "Yellows and Youth, Our Struggles Meet," and the students joined an ongoing French grievance: affordability. The cost of living, fuel prices pushed up by the Iran war, pensions, wages, and the sense that the state taxes like a Scandinavian nation and provides services like a Mediterranean one. Fifteen hundred shops were destroyed and 3,000 were looted. The government is blaming the far left, the far left is blaming the police, and the only thing everybody in the street agrees on is that the solution to these problems is more money. And that's why I struggle to see an easy solution. There's simple arithmetic that doesn't care about the placards. Every euro for a teacher is a euro the bond market expects to see cut somewhere else. The protesters are asking the state to do what the bond market has said not to do. The comparison everyone reaches for is the 1968 French "revolution," when students took to the streets, a government was on its heels, and the president suddenly looked old. I think the analogy is wrong, or at least incomplete. Why? Because de Gaulle dissolved the Assembly and called snap elections that he won, France's public debt was a fraction of its GDP, and the country had room to spend its way to calm. Let's not forget that they raised the minimum wage by more than 30%. Macron has none of the options that de Gaulle had. Could he dissolve the Assembly again? Sure, but the last time he tried that, he produced the hung parliament that has contributed to today's problems. He can't spend to solve the problem, because the bond market is watching. He can't credibly promise reform, because his government is the fourth since the last election. And the political calendar means every group (Le Pen's National Rally, Melenchon's France Unbowed, and the Socialists) is laser-focused on positioning, not governing. Several of my friends who think deeply about geopolitics and geoeconomics have suggested that if the upcoming budget fails, France might have to seek assistance from the International Monetary Fund. The IMF. For France. The ECB, meanwhile, has suggested the solution to French problems lies in France. (Christine Lagarde recently noted that "the primary and first solution lies at home in France.") Some of my friends in Europe are more relaxed about this drama, noting that France is "too big to fail." Others suggest it's too big to save. The next six weeks decide a lot. The Assembly votes on the revenue half of the budget in early November and on the whole package around November 17. There's a fascinating constitutional provision that allows a bill to pass without a vote. Will Lecornu, despite assurances he would never use this provision (Article 49.3), opt for this path? If he does, which seems likely, what happens? I believe there are three main possibilities: First , France could muddle through until the upcoming April elections, the government could make some token gestures such as a school reform package, and the real decisions can be deferred until the next administration takes office. Indeed, this is the default path that France seems to revert to but leads to ever higher debt, higher interest to service that debt, and a population that believes the way to get things done is via protest. I believe this is the most likely scenario. Second , the government falls apart because of the budget. This scenario probably means an emergency law keeps spending the same, leading to a sovereign debt crisis, a bailout, and dragging Italy and Spain along for the ride. At that point, France would have to either choose submission to an EU or IMF dictated program or pursue a Brexit style defiance of Brussels. The third scenario is that the budget leads to real reform. Think of this as a real plan to invest in schools, funded by real cuts. The bond market would love this, spreads would plunge, and France's vicious cycle could turn virtuous. Unfortunately, I think this is the least likely scenario. The question for the rest of Europe and for global markets is whether it stays contained. I don't think it does, for three reasons: 1. France is critical to the euro 's architecture. The eurozone has always been understood as a core and a periphery, with Germany and France as the core and the crisis-era rescues flowing outward. When France has to raise money more richly than does Italy, the core-periphery map stops making sense. The ECB would have to address problems that it was not designed to address: a potential failure at the core. Its crisis tool are designed to help small countries hit by unwarranted panic, not for a large country whose panic is warranted. 2. The bond vigilantes reassert control. France emerges as the first large democracy where the market forced the question of what happens when you can neither raise taxes nor cut spending (nor inflate). The honest answer, the one on display in Paris, is: you pay more, until you can't. The lesson will spread wide and far, and quickly. Expect bond market contagion. 3. Political ramifications will also spread quickly. Within days of Creteil, students in Belgium blockaded schools; Italian students declared a "No Meloni Day" and rioting spread across Milan; Greek students pitched tents outside parliament in Athens; students in Tirana attacked the education ministry. Milei's university cuts led millions in Argentina into the streets, and in Germany, there are calls for protests in 21 cities on October 31. The narrative war over what the French unrest is about (fiscal failure, far-left agitation, inbound migration, police brutality) is already a transatlantic one, and whoever wins it will shape elections from Madrid to Berlin. Zhou Enlai was right. It is too early to say how this ends. But a bond market at 5% portends trouble. | | ---|---|--- VIKRAM MANSHARAMANI is an entrepreneur, consultant, scholar, neighbor, husband, father, volunteer, and professional generalist who thinks in multiple-dimensions and looks beyond the short-term. LinkedIn has twice listed him as its #1 Top Voice in Money & Finance, and Worth profiled him as one of the 100 Most Powerful People in Global Finance. Vikram earned a PhD From MIT, has taught at Yale and Harvard, and is the author of three books, , and . body:
People called it brave. I called it the job.

---
| | [](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/142178528/656050254/-373287771?refcode=EM_BS_LUR_261025_FR_Guts_A0_na_U1_X2_M4&amount=5&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMzAvMS85MDA3OCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICIzY2E2MjAwNC1jY2QwLWYxMTEtYmY1Yi0wMDIyNDgyOWY4NjkiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=77gvR_8i4g1uUtR1WF94OCm5-Qm9Khsj2nKE1JaZ66I=) On the five-year anniversary of the attack on the Capitol, I testified to Congress about what happened that day. A lot of folks told me afterward that it took guts. But I’ll be honest with you: I knew exactly what speaking out could cost, because I’d already paid it once. When I served on the January 6th Committee in 2022, my family and I became targets. We received threats. Armed people endangered our neighbors. Someone tried to break into our home. The sheriff assigned a deputy to stand guard for months. But I’d make the same choice again. Call it guts if you want. I’ve got plenty left for this fight. # **NINE DAYS LEFT**
Dear Friends & Neighbors,

I am the product of the American Dream. Trust me, it's worth fighting for.

My opponent was born on third base and thinks she hit a triple.

Don't just take my word for it.

This Wednesday at 8:00 PM, I'll debate Maggie Goodlander live on WMUR. Here's my prediction: she'll stick to the same old party talking points, and I'll spend the night laying out my plan to lower your costs. I trust you to be the judge.

Nine days. Let's leave everything on the field.
THIS PAST WEEK...
# **I WON THE NEW ENGLAND COLLEGE DEBATE!**
In Henniker, I went head to head with Maggie Goodlander, and I came with plans, not talking points.

When the moderators asked how I'd bring down the cost of healthcare, I laid it out: [Watch my one-minute answer here.](https://us.list-manage.com/uEVLV8QmEPU?e=c338950e03&c2id=adf8b61e01be85c238f26a96cfd7c41c)

Thank you to everyone who [stood out with me on the Henniker common](https://us.list-manage.com/18j4nvRP9Ll?e=c338950e03&c2id=adf8b61e01be85c238f26a96cfd7c41c) beforehand!
# **KEENE STATE, NASHUA & THE SUPER CHASE**
On Wednesday, I [took questions from students at Keene State](https://us.list-manage.com/xcxKibmeInR?e=c338950e03&c2id=adf8b61e01be85c238f26a96cfd7c41c), because young people especially deserve to be heard.

On Thursday, Granite Staters filled my 10th "Ask Me Anything" Town Hall at Nashua Community College, and [here's what a few of them had to say](https://us.list-manage.com/PgJXoBhNEOA?e=c338950e03&c2id=adf8b61e01be85c238f26a96cfd7c41c).

On Saturday, Team Lily [hit the doors with Turning Point Action's Super Chase](https://us.list-manage.com/14IscByWpcH?e=c338950e03&c2id=adf8b61e01be85c238f26a96cfd7c41c) in Newport and Nashua.

# 9 DAYS TO GO...
**DEBATE NIGHT**

# **WEDNESDAY 10/28, 8:00 PM - WATCH MY WMUR DEBATE**
This is the big one: my debate against Maggie Goodlander, live on WMUR, in front of the whole state. Wherever you are in the country, you can watch it with me.

**[WATCH LIVE ON WMUR.COM](https://us.list-manage.com/GpNRBelbJt8?e=c338950e03&c2id=adf8b61e01be85c238f26a96cfd7c41c)**
(or on WMUR News 9 in New Hampshire)

**Then help me spread the word.** Many Granite Staters are still making up their minds. If you know anyone in New Hampshire, send them the debate and ask them to be the judge. A text from someone they trust goes further than any ad. **IN NEW HAMPSHIRE? JOIN ME IN MANCHESTER.**
Wave signs with me outside WMUR, 100 S Commercial St. Please arrive by 4:45 PM, before the 5:45 sunset. [RSVP here](https://us.list-manage.com/vMgukw1_3qm?e=c338950e03&c2id=adf8b61e01be85c238f26a96cfd7c41c) for all the details.

body:
[ stdin# ]Josh Shapiro for Pennsylvania
Derek, I sat down
with Dana Bash on CNN about how low JD Vance and his allies have stooped
during these midterms.

Hear me when I say: No one has stooped lower than the profoundly and
pathetically weak excuse of a Vice President we have in JD Vance.

Before I say any more: I don’t even want to be writing this email. I’m
tired of this, you’re tired of this, we’re all tired of the disgusting
lack of morals shown by JD Vance and his allies.

[ https://act.joshshapiro.org/go/20796?t=1001&akid=777%2E245147%2EwVWlc4 ]But they’re getting dangerously close to winning in key races up and
down the ballot — including right here in Pennsylvania. Please, will you
rush a donation right now to help me reject this politics of the lowest
common denominator?

[ https://act.joshshapiro.org/go/20796?t=1002&akid=777%2E245147%2EwVWlc4 ]Pitch In →

Look, everywhere JD Vance goes, he puts on a phony act and chastises all
of us about “morality” and “respectable politics.”

But then he turns around and shows us what little morality he actually
practices.

The truth is,
Derek: JD Vance has no core. He
does whatever his boss tells him to do. He makes lame excuses for
Republican candidates’ disgusting attack ads. And when everything fails,
he begs and pleads with voters to give Republicans “another chance.”

It all speaks to the lack of character being pushed by Donald Trump, JD
Vance, and those who stand faithfully beside this corrupt administration.
And in just nine days, we need to send them the strongest rejection
possible.

[ https://act.joshshapiro.org/go/20796?t=1003&akid=777%2E245147%2EwVWlc4 ]Derek, this
isn’t a message I can send alone. So please, if you’re sick and tired of
low-level politics plaguing our elections, plugging up our systems, and
making life harder for working families everywhere, I’m humbly asking you:
Will you pitch in $5, $25, or whatever you can to help me fight back?

If you've saved your payment information with ActBlue Express, your
donation will go through immediately:

Thank you,

Josh Shapiro
